cases.alertTitle: Encoded PowerShell on a finance workstation
cases.detectionRule: EDR · powershell.exe launched with -EncodedCommand

evidence.detail: Lineage: WINWORD.EXE → cmd.exe → powershell.exe. A document spawned a shell — not how IT runs scripts.
evidence.label: Parent is WINWORD.EXE

evidence.detail: Decoded blob is an in-memory downloader: pull a follow-on script from a remote host and run it without writing to disk.
evidence.label: Decodes to a download-cradle

evidence.detail: Within 2s of execution: outbound HTTPS to a domain in no proxy category, first-seen org-wide.
evidence.label: Immediate outbound to a fresh domain

evidence.detail: No maintenance window, no change record for FIN-WS-04. jdoe is Finance, not IT — no reason to run admin scripts.
evidence.label: No change ticket

evidence.detail: The callout domain was registered 72h ago; one feed already tags it suspicious.
evidence.label: Domain registered 3 days ago

evidence.detail: jdoe received an 'overdue invoice' attachment 9 minutes before execution. Plausible initial-access vector.
evidence.label: Phishy invoice email just before

learn.concept: Encoded ≠ malicious. Decode it, then read the parent process and what it did. Office → PowerShell → outbound is a classic initial-access chain; a sanctioned tool with a change ticket is not.
learn.pointer: MITRE ATT&CK T1059.001 · LetsDefend 'Detecting Malicious PowerShell'

cases.trigger: powershell.exe spawned with -EncodedCommand on FIN-WS-04 at 02:14 local — off-hours.
cases.why: Encoding was never the threat — the LINEAGE and BEHAVIOUR are. A Word document spawned PowerShell, the decoded payload is an in-memory download-cradle, there's a live outbound to a 3-day-old domain, and no change ticket on a finance host off-hours. That's an active initial-access chain: isolate the host and escalate to IR.

cases.alertTitle: Failed-logon burst then success — user rkhan
cases.detectionRule: SIEM · ≥10× 4625 then a 4624 from the same source within 5m

evidence.detail: Every 4625 originates from MKT-WS-03 (corporate subnet), clustered in 90s, logon type 2 (interactive at the keyboard). Then a clean 4624.
evidence.label: All from rkhan's own workstation

evidence.detail: Ticket from rkhan at 09:03: 'forgot my password after the weekend forced reset.' Two minutes before the success.
evidence.label: Helpdesk ticket: forgot password

evidence.detail: Source is the office LAN; rkhan's normal location. No VPN, no foreign IP, no impossible travel.
evidence.label: No remote access

evidence.detail: No 4672. rkhan is a standard user; nothing elevated.
evidence.label: No privilege events

evidence.detail: Source is an RFC1918 corporate address; no external reputation to look up.
evidence.label: Internal IP — nothing to enrich

evidence.detail: A months-old phishing report mentions a domain resembling the company's. It pattern-matches if you squint, but it has nothing to do with this logon — a red herring.
evidence.label: Old lookalike-domain report

evidence.detail: Org-wide weekend password reset was scheduled (CHG-2270) — it explains the failures; it authorizes nothing.
evidence.label: Reset — not a grant

learn.concept: The 4625-burst → 4624 pattern is only a threat when the source/time/account don't fit the user. Always check WHERE it came from before escalating — same detection, opposite verdict.
learn.pointer: Windows Security event-log analysis · tune the rule to exclude same-host interactive failures

cases.trigger: 12× failed logons (4625) then a success (4624) for rkhan at 09:05, Monday morning.
cases.why: Same shape as a password-guessing hit — failures then a success — but the SOURCE and CONTEXT flip the verdict. The failures are fat-fingered attempts from the user's OWN keyboard right after a scheduled weekend reset, with a helpdesk ticket to match, then a normal interactive logon. The rule matched the shape, but nobody was guessing — what it hunts for never happened. Close FP.

cases.alertTitle: Encoded PowerShell on a patch server
cases.detectionRule: EDR · powershell.exe launched with -EncodedCommand

evidence.detail: Lineage: ccmexec.exe (SCCM/patch-management agent) → powershell.exe, under service account svc-sccm. A known IT automation tool, not a document.
evidence.label: Parent is the SCCM agent

evidence.detail: Decoded blob enumerates installed updates and reports compliance — a routine patch/inventory task.
evidence.label: Decodes to an inventory script

evidence.detail: Standing change CHG-2291 authorizes automated nightly patching on SRV-PATCH-02 in this exact window.
evidence.label: Approved change CHG-2291

evidence.detail: Connections go to the internal update server (known-good); no external callouts.
evidence.label: Outbound to internal WSUS only

evidence.detail: No external indicators; all destinations internal and reputable.
evidence.label: Nothing flagged

evidence.detail: svc-sccm is a non-interactive service account scoped to patch management.
evidence.label: Service account, not a person

learn.concept: Benign True Positive = correct detection of AUTHORIZED activity. Separate it from a False Positive — there, the flagged behaviour never happened at all, so no ticket could sanction it. Don't suppress a rule just because today's hit was sanctioned.
learn.pointer: Microsoft Defender alert classification · TP vs FP vs Benign-TP

cases.trigger: powershell.exe -EncodedCommand on SRV-PATCH-02 at 03:00 — inside the nightly maintenance window.
cases.why: The detection was RIGHT — that really is encoded PowerShell — but the parent is the patch-management agent and a standing change ticket authorizes it. That's a Benign True Positive, not a False Positive: the rule didn't misfire, the activity was simply sanctioned. Closing it as 'FP' would be wrong reasoning (and would tempt someone to suppress the rule that correctly catches the malicious version in A1).

cases.alertTitle: Periodic DNS to high-entropy domains
cases.detectionRule: SIEM · regular-interval DNS to algorithmically-generated domains (DGA heuristic)

evidence.detail: Queries fire on a near-exact 60s cadence; labels are long high-entropy strings across many unrelated registrations; most return NXDOMAIN with the occasional resolve; rare TLDs (.top/.xyz).
evidence.label: Fixed-interval, high-entropy, NXDOMAIN bursts

evidence.detail: The queries come from an unsigned binary running out of %TEMP% — not the system resolver, not a browser.
evidence.label: A temp-path binary, not a browser

evidence.detail: After each resolve: a small fixed-size outbound POST. The hallmark of a beacon check-in, not human browsing.
evidence.label: Small, regular, equal-sized POSTs

evidence.detail: Of the resolving domains, one matches a tracked C2 infrastructure feed.
evidence.label: One domain on a C2 feed

evidence.detail: No change/asset record for this binary; software inventory shows it isn't an approved application.
evidence.label: No authorized tooling

learn.concept: DNS C2 tells: regular timing (beaconing), long high-entropy domains (DGA), NXDOMAIN bursts, rare TLDs — but always confirm the PROCESS making the queries isn't a browser or the resolver. Behaviour, then attribution.
learn.pointer: MITRE ATT&CK T1071.004 · DNS log analysis, entropy/DGA detection

cases.trigger: ENG-LAP-09 queries a rotating set of long, random-looking domains every ~60s, around the clock.
cases.why: Fixed-interval queries (beaconing), high-entropy domains across many registrations (DGA), NXDOMAIN bursts, rare TLDs — and crucially the queries come from an unsigned temp-path binary with small regular outbound POSTs. That's command-and-control, not browsing. Isolate the host and escalate.

cases.alertTitle: Failed-logon burst then success — user msmith
cases.detectionRule: SIEM · ≥20× 4625 then a 4624 from the same source within 5m

evidence.detail: 37× 4625 against this one account from a single external IP in 4 minutes — guessing in depth — then a 4624 success, logon type 3 (network) over the VPN.
evidence.label: Brute-force burst then a hit

evidence.detail: Source IP geolocates to a country msmith has never used; the success lands minutes apart from msmith's last normal logon in the home country — too far to travel between the two. Impossible travel.
evidence.label: Impossible travel

evidence.detail: Minutes after the logon, a 4672 (special privileges assigned) fires for msmith — an account that shouldn't be elevating.
evidence.label: 4672 right after success

evidence.detail: The external IP appears on a known brute-force / password-guessing feed.
evidence.label: Source IP on a brute-force list

evidence.detail: No pentest authorization or RoE covering credential testing against VPN-GW this window.
evidence.label: No authorized testing

evidence.detail: HR calendar shows msmith on leave all week — shouldn't be logging in at all.
evidence.label: User is on PTO

learn.concept: 4625 = failed logon (a deep burst against one account = brute-force/password-guessing), 4624 = success, 4672 = special privileges. The signature is burst→success from an anomalous source/time. Correlate source IP / time / account — and check whether the user should even be active.
learn.pointer: MITRE ATT&CK T1110.001 · Splunk/Sentinel auth detections

cases.trigger: 37× failed logons (4625) then a success (4624) for msmith from a foreign ASN at 03:40.
cases.why: A 4625 burst → 4624 success from a foreign IP, impossible travel (two logons too far apart to be one person), a 4672 elevation right after, source IP on a brute-force feed, no authorized-testing ticket, and the user is on PTO. That's a confirmed account compromise — disable the account / isolate the session and escalate to IR now.

cases.alertTitle: DGA heuristic fired on marketing laptop
cases.detectionRule: SIEM · regular-interval DNS to algorithmically-generated domains (DGA heuristic)

evidence.detail: The random-looking labels are all subdomains of a single well-known CDN / anti-bot parent domain. Every query resolves cleanly — no NXDOMAIN bursts — and timing is bursty with user activity, not a fixed beacon.
evidence.label: Subdomains of ONE reputable CDN

evidence.detail: The queries come from chrome.exe and a known analytics SDK — normal web components, not an unknown binary.
evidence.label: It's the browser

evidence.detail: The CDN parent domain has a long history and clean reputation across feeds.
evidence.label: Parent domain is clean

evidence.detail: Months ago, one of the CDN's many shared IPs also hosted something later flagged. That's shared-hosting coincidence, not this host's traffic — tempting, irrelevant.
evidence.label: One historical IP overlap

evidence.detail: Variable-sized HTTPS tied to page loads; no fixed-size periodic check-ins.
evidence.label: Ordinary web traffic

evidence.detail: No change relevant; this is end-user browsing.
evidence.label: n/a

learn.concept: DGA heuristics over-fire on CDNs and anti-bot subdomains. Discriminate: one parent domain vs many registrations, clean resolution vs NXDOMAIN bursts, browser vs unknown process, activity-driven vs fixed-interval timing. Then tune the rule.
learn.pointer: Entropy/DGA detection · allow-list known CDN parents to cut the noise

cases.trigger: MKT-WS-12 makes frequent queries to long, random-looking subdomains.
cases.why: The 'high-entropy domains' are CDN / anti-bot subdomains under one reputable parent, resolving cleanly, queried irregularly by a browser. That's ordinary modern web traffic — the DGA heuristic over-fired. The discriminators against C1: one parent vs many registrations, clean resolution vs NXDOMAIN bursts, browser vs temp-path binary, activity-driven vs fixed interval.

cases.alertTitle: Credential spray across many accounts
cases.detectionRule: SIEM · 4625 across ≥15 accounts from one source, with some 4624 successes

evidence.detail: One internal source, 23 accounts, one password each, then 3 successes. This IS attack behaviour — the detection is correct.
evidence.label: Textbook spray — and it worked

evidence.detail: Authorization CHG-2310 / signed RoE covers credential testing from PENTEST-01 this week. Deconfliction note names the testing team.
evidence.label: Approved pentest CHG-2310

evidence.detail: PENTEST-01 is an internal, inventoried host on the security team's segment.
evidence.label: Internal source

evidence.detail: Internal source; no external reputation in play.
evidence.label: Nothing external

evidence.detail: Security calendar shows an authorized engagement running this week.
evidence.label: Testing window confirmed

learn.concept: Authorized attack activity (a sanctioned pentest) is a Benign True Positive, not a False Positive and not something to escalate. Check for a deconfliction / RoE record before you act — and document it so the next analyst doesn't re-fire on the same engagement.
learn.pointer: Purple-team deconfliction · 'is this us or someone else?'

cases.trigger: A spray across 23 accounts then 3 successes, all from one internal host, 14:00 on a Wednesday.
cases.why: This looks exactly like an attack because it IS attack behaviour — but there's a signed pentest authorization covering this host and window. That's the cleanest Benign True Positive there is: a correct detection of AUTHORIZED activity. (It's also the bridge to the red team's world: same tradecraft, opposite verdict.) Escalating it wastes IR; isolating PENTEST-01 would blow up a sanctioned engagement. Confirm the RoE, note it on the ticket, close benign.

cases.alertTitle: Reported phishing — credential harvest impersonating IT
cases.detectionRule: Defender for Office 365 · user-reported + URL re-scored suspicious

evidence.detail: SPF fail, DKIM none, DMARC none/fail — the visible From impersonates a trusted brand but aligns with nothing that authenticated it. (Corroborates the look-alike; a look-alike can pass its OWN auth, so this isn't the verdict by itself.)
evidence.label: Doesn't align with the brand it imitates

evidence.detail: Sender domain registered 6 days ago — a look-alike of the brand it imitates, not the corporate mail domain.
evidence.label: Week-old look-alike domain

evidence.detail: The link resolves to a fake corporate-login page — a form that captures whatever's typed and sends it onward. A harvester, not a real portal.
evidence.label: Credential-harvesting landing page

evidence.detail: The harvester domain appears on two phishing-URL feeds.
evidence.label: Landing domain on phishing feeds

evidence.detail: pdavis reported it before clicking; no anomalous sign-in for the account. Caught early.
evidence.label: No creds entered (yet)

evidence.detail: A security-awareness phishing simulation runs this quarter — but its register shows no send to pdavis and a different sending platform. Tempting, but not this.
evidence.label: There IS an awareness campaign…

learn.concept: Authentication answers 'did the From domain authenticate ITSELF' — not 'is this safe'. The decisive tells are the look-alike domain + the credential-harvest page + that it's in no campaign register; SPF/DKIM authenticate and DMARC governs disposition + From-alignment, but a look-alike can pass its own auth. (The visible From check is DMARC alignment, not raw SPF/DKIM.)
learn.pointer: MITRE ATT&CK T1566 · LetsDefend 'Phishing Email Analysis'

cases.trigger: A user forwarded an 'IT: your mailbox is over quota — verify now' email; the gateway re-scored the link as suspicious.
cases.why: Nothing authenticated the message (SPF/DKIM/DMARC all fail, From unaligned), the sender is a week-old look-alike, and the link is a live credential-harvesting page on two phishing feeds. It is NOT the sanctioned simulation — that campaign never targeted this user and uses a different platform. Real phish, no creds entered yet: escalate, block the sender/URL, and hunt for anyone who did click.

cases.alertTitle: Atypical travel — sign-in from two countries
cases.detectionRule: Entra ID Protection · risky sign-in (unlikelyTravel)

evidence.detail: The 'foreign' IP belongs to the company VPN egress range — already used by dozens of staff, just never added to Named locations.
evidence.label: It's the corporate VPN egress

evidence.detail: Both sign-ins are from rwong's registered, compliant laptop, the normal client app and the usual user-agent. Only the egress IP differs.
evidence.label: Same device, app, user-agent

evidence.detail: Detection is unlikelyTravel (Entra-native), risk Medium; the account is still inside its 14-day / 10-login learning window where these FPs are expected.
evidence.label: Atypical travel, in learning window

evidence.detail: The egress IP has clean reputation.
evidence.label: VPN IP is clean

evidence.detail: rwong has an approved trip abroad next month — unrelated to today's sign-in.
evidence.label: Upcoming trip abroad

learn.concept: Atypical/impossible travel over-fires on VPNs and during the 14-day/10-login learning period. Validate the sign-in fields — registered device, app, location, IP, user-agent — before you call it; a corporate VPN egress → confirm safe + add to Named locations.
learn.pointer: Entra ID Protection investigate-risk · Named locations

cases.trigger: rwong signed in from the office, then from a neighbouring country the account has never used before — flagged as atypical travel.
cases.why: Same shape as a compromise, but the 'impossible' location is the corporate VPN egress: a registered, compliant device, normal app and user-agent — only the IP differs — and the account is still in its learning window. Confirm the sign-in safe and add the VPN range to Named locations so it stops firing. The detection misfired; close FP.

cases.alertTitle: EDR: offensive-security tool detected
cases.detectionRule: Defender for Endpoint · 'hacktool' / behavioral detection

evidence.detail: Change CHG-3120 authorizes a red-team engagement on SEC-LAB-02 this week; the tool and host are named in the signed RoE / deconfliction note.
evidence.label: Approved red-team engagement

evidence.detail: AlertEvidence: the binary is a well-known security-testing tool, on the security team's lab host SEC-LAB-02, run by a security-team account.
evidence.label: Security-team lab box

evidence.detail: Lineage shows an interactive launch by the tester — not spawned from a document or a temp-path dropper.
evidence.label: Launched interactively by the tester

evidence.detail: The hash is 'known', but it's a legitimate dual-use offensive-security utility, not malware.
evidence.label: Dual-use, not malware-by-author

evidence.detail: The account belongs to the security team.
evidence.label: Security-team account

learn.concept: An authorized red-team / security-test tool is a Benign True Positive ('Informational, expected activity'), not malware to escalate. Check the engagement/change ticket and deconfliction note first; suppress for the window — don't kill the rule that catches the real thing.
learn.pointer: Defender for Endpoint classification: Informational, expected activity (Security test)

cases.trigger: Defender flagged a known offensive-security tool running on SEC-LAB-02.
cases.why: The detection is correct — that really is an offensive-security tool — but it's running inside an authorized red-team engagement on the security team's own lab box, named in the change ticket and RoE. That's Defender's 'Informational, expected activity' / Benign-TP: classify benign and suppress for the engagement window; don't escalate (you'd burn IR and blow the test), and don't permanently whitelist the rule. Isolating SEC-LAB-02 would break a sanctioned exercise. (A red-team engagement's run, seen from the blue chair.)

cases.alertTitle: User reported suspicious MFA activity
cases.detectionRule: Entra ID Protection · userReportedSuspiciousActivity

evidence.detail: A burst of MFA push prompts to tkaur's authenticator at 01:50, none tied to a sign-in she started; she denied and reported them. Classic MFA fatigue.
evidence.label: Prompt bombing, denied + reported

evidence.detail: Alongside it, a passwordSpray detection on tkaur — which fires ONLY once the attacker has validated the correct password. The credential is already compromised.
evidence.label: passwordSpray means the password is known

evidence.detail: The attempts driving the prompts come from an anonymized IP on an unregistered device, off-hours.
evidence.label: Anonymized IP, unregistered device

evidence.detail: The source IP is on a credential-attack feed.
evidence.label: Source on a credential-attack feed

evidence.detail: The source isn't a sanctioned VPN or a known duty location.
evidence.label: Not a known VPN/duty IP

learn.concept: MFA fatigue = unsolicited prompt-bombing hoping the user taps approve. 'User reported suspicious activity' fires on a denied+reported prompt; a paired passwordSpray means the password is already known. Treat as compromise — reset + revoke, don't just dismiss the prompts.
learn.pointer: MITRE T1621 / T1078 · enable Authenticator number-matching

cases.trigger: tkaur tapped 'No, it's not me' on a flood of MFA push prompts at 01:50 that she never started, and reported them.
cases.why: She denied and reported prompts she never started — MFA fatigue — and the paired passwordSpray detection only fires once the attacker has the correct password, so the credential is already compromised and they're hammering MFA to get in. Confirm compromised: disable the account, force a reset, revoke sessions, escalate to IR. (Number-matching / login-context in Authenticator is what stops the fatigue working.)

cases.alertTitle: Large outbound transfer to cloud storage
cases.detectionRule: DLP / proxy · high-volume egress to cloud storage

evidence.detail: A standing change authorizes nightly backup of this share to the CORPORATE cloud tenant in exactly this window.
evidence.label: Standing backup change CHG-2980

evidence.detail: The transfer is the sanctioned backup product (not an ad-hoc script), under svc-backup, to the corporate tenant — not a personal account.
evidence.label: Backup agent → corporate tenant

evidence.detail: DLP matched on volume/class, but the destination is the approved corporate backup target.
evidence.label: Matched on volume, approved target

evidence.detail: The process is the backup product's signed binary, on its schedule.
evidence.label: Signed, scheduled backup binary

evidence.detail: Destination is the corporate cloud tenant; clean reputation.
evidence.label: Corporate tenant, clean

learn.concept: A scheduled backup or sanctioned cloud-sync to the CORPORATE tenant is a Benign-TP, not exfil. Discriminate on process (backup product vs ad-hoc script), destination (corporate vs personal cloud), and a change ticket — then add a DLP exclusion for the approved path.
learn.pointer: DLP exclusions · authorized-backup path

cases.trigger: A service account moved a large volume of data to cloud storage overnight.
cases.why: Same DLP/egress trigger as exfil, opposite verdict: it's the sanctioned nightly backup — the approved backup agent under the backup service account, to the CORPORATE tenant, covered by a standing change ticket. Correct detection of authorized activity = Benign-TP. Note it and close benign; escalating would page IR for a backup. Tells vs real exfil: signed backup product (not ad-hoc script), corporate destination (not personal), and a change ticket.

cases.alertTitle: EDR: malware that executed on an endpoint
cases.detectionRule: Defender for Endpoint · behavioral + AV detection

evidence.detail: AlertEvidence (DetectionSource=Antivirus, ServiceSource=Defender for Endpoint): an unsigned binary in %TEMP%, status NOT quarantined — it executed.
evidence.label: Unsigned temp-path binary, NOT quarantined

evidence.detail: Lineage: a mail attachment → the binary → it wrote a Run key and a scheduled task, then reached out. Persistence established.
evidence.label: Mail attachment → persistence

evidence.detail: Regular-interval outbound to a first-seen domain right after execution — beacon-like.
evidence.label: Beaconing to a fresh domain

evidence.detail: Both the file hash and the callout domain are on malware feeds.
evidence.label: Hash + domain known-bad

evidence.detail: No change record; ENG-WS-21 isn't a security/test host and nbianchi isn't IT.
evidence.label: No change, not a test box

evidence.detail: nbianchi changed teams recently — irrelevant to the detection.
evidence.label: Recently changed teams

learn.concept: EDR triage: read AlertEvidence for the file + quarantine state, then the process tree for lineage and persistence (Run keys / scheduled tasks), then network for C2. 'Not quarantined' + persistence + beacon = it executed and is live → isolate.
learn.pointer: MITRE ATT&CK · Defender for Endpoint AlertEvidence table

cases.trigger: Defender flagged a suspicious binary on ENG-WS-21; AlertEvidence shows it ran and is not yet contained.
cases.why: An unsigned temp-path binary that actually executed (not quarantined), spawned from a mail attachment, set up persistence (Run key + scheduled task), and is beaconing to a flagged domain — hash and domain both known-bad, no change ticket. That's a live infection: isolate the host and escalate to IR. (Most EDR remediation is reversible — you can restore a quarantined file later if it turns out benign.)

cases.alertTitle: Reported phishing — 'Q3 bonus, confirm details'
cases.detectionRule: Defender for Office 365 · user-reported

evidence.detail: The awareness register shows an ACTIVE authorized phishing-simulation campaign this week, from the sanctioned platform, targeting exactly this user group — subject 'Q3 bonus'.
evidence.label: Active authorized simulation

evidence.detail: SPF/DKIM/DMARC pass for the simulation platform's domain — consistent with the register. (Auth-pass alone never proves benign; the register makes the call.)
evidence.label: Authenticates to the sim platform

evidence.detail: The lure domain is owned by the awareness vendor — not a look-alike of a real corporate brand.
evidence.label: Vendor lure domain, not a look-alike

evidence.detail: The link goes to the training platform's tracking/teaching page, not a live credential harvester.
evidence.label: Training 'gotcha' page

evidence.detail: No external malicious indicators.
evidence.label: No malicious indicators

learn.concept: A sanctioned phishing simulation is a Benign True Positive: the email really is phishing-shaped, but it's authorized. The campaign register is the proof — NOT the auth result (a real phish can pass its own auth, and sims are often allow-listed while failing it). Check the register before escalating user reports — and still credit the report.
learn.pointer: Microsoft Attack Simulation Training / KnowBe4 · TP vs B-TP

cases.trigger: Several users reported a 'Q3 bonus — confirm your details' email with a login link.
cases.why: The reporters were right — it IS a phishing-shaped email. But it's the org's own sanctioned awareness simulation: the register shows an active authorized run from the training platform to this exact group, and the mail authenticates to that platform. Correct detection of authorized activity = Benign-TP. Don't escalate (you'd waste IR and tip off the test); note it and close benign — and the reports are exactly the behaviour the simulation trains.

cases.alertTitle: Possible exfiltration to personal cloud storage
cases.detectionRule: Defender for Cloud Apps / DLP · unusual upload to cloud storage

evidence.detail: An unusual process (powershell.exe) read large local files at 02:30, then made HTTPS POSTs to a PERSONAL cloud-storage account — not the corporate tenant.
evidence.label: Ad-hoc process → personal cloud

evidence.detail: The files matched the 'PII / financial-records' DLP policy; the volume is far above this user's normal.
evidence.label: Classified data, far above baseline

evidence.detail: powershell.exe wasn't launched by a backup product — it's an ad-hoc script, off-hours.
evidence.label: Not a backup product

evidence.detail: The destination is a personal cloud-storage endpoint with no business relationship to the company.
evidence.label: No business relationship

evidence.detail: No backup or data-migration change record covers this transfer.
evidence.label: No backup/migration change

learn.concept: Exfil to cloud storage (T1567.002) blends into normal cloud traffic — a common cloud service, often a personal account the host doesn't normally use. The read: unusual process + large reads + HTTPS POST to cloud storage + off-hours + DLP class + above baseline. The discriminator vs a benign backup is destination (personal vs corporate) and whether a backup/sync is authorized.
learn.pointer: MITRE ATT&CK T1567.002 · Defender for Cloud Apps anomaly alerts

cases.trigger: Off-hours, a script on FIN-WS-08 read a large batch of classified finance files and POSTed them to a personal cloud-storage account.
cases.why: Hallmark exfil: an unusual process (powershell, not a backup product) reading large classified files off-hours and POSTing them to a PERSONAL cloud account with no business relationship, far above baseline, no change ticket. Adversaries hide exfil in cloud storage the host already uses — but the personal destination + DLP class + volume give it away. Contain and escalate to IR.

cases.alertTitle: Repeated account lockouts — user achen
cases.detectionRule: SIEM · Event 4740 (account locked out) ×6 in an hour

evidence.detail: Correlating 4771/4776: every failure traces to achen's phone (ActiveSync) and a mapped drive — both still submitting the OLD password from before the weekend reset.
evidence.label: Bad passwords come from achen's OWN devices

evidence.detail: Ticket from achen right after the scheduled weekend reset: 'my account keeps locking every few minutes.'
evidence.label: Helpdesk ticket: 'keeps locking'

evidence.detail: The 4740s repeat, but the Caller Computer Name is blank — the true source only shows once you correlate 4771/4776.
evidence.label: 4740 fires, Caller Computer Name blank

evidence.detail: The org-wide weekend password reset (CHG-4102) lines up with when the lockouts started — timing, not authorization.
evidence.label: Weekend reset explains the timing

evidence.detail: Every source is internal; nothing external to enrich.
evidence.label: All internal

evidence.detail: A single failure once came from an unfamiliar subnet — but it resolves to the corporate VPN pool, not an attacker.
evidence.label: One failure from an odd subnet

evidence.detail: HR calendar shows achen on a normal in-office day — nothing anomalous about the account being in use.
evidence.label: User active, in office

learn.concept: Most account lockouts aren't an attack — a device caching an OLD password after a change. Event 4740's Caller Computer Name is often blank; correlate Kerberos 4771 / NTLM 4776 to find the true source. Escalate only when that source is anomalous/external.
learn.pointer: Microsoft event-4740 · 4771/4776 correlation to find the lockout source

cases.trigger: achen's account has locked out six times since the weekend password reset.
cases.why: The #1 real cause of lockouts, and it looks alarming until you read it right. Event 4740's Caller Computer Name is blank, so you correlate 4771/4776 — and the bad passwords all come from achen's OWN phone and a mapped drive, still submitting the pre-reset password after the weekend change. No attack; a stale cached credential. Close FP, and have the user update the stored password everywhere it's cached.

cases.alertTitle: Account lockouts across many users
cases.detectionRule: SIEM · Event 4740 across ≥10 accounts within minutes

evidence.detail: 4771/4776 failures across 10+ accounts from a single external IP in minutes — a credential attack noisy enough to trip each account's lockout threshold. The lockouts are collateral of the attack.
evidence.label: Failures across 10+ accounts from one external IP

evidence.detail: No penetration-test authorization or credential-testing RoE covers this window.
evidence.label: No authorized testing

evidence.detail: The external source IP appears on a credential-attack feed.
evidence.label: Source on a credential-attack feed

evidence.detail: 4740 across many accounts within the same short window — not one user's device.
evidence.label: Many accounts, near-simultaneous

evidence.detail: The source geolocates to a country none of these users log in from.
evidence.label: Foreign origin

evidence.detail: The affected accounts are a spread of active users, none on leave — not one person's cached device.
evidence.label: Targeted users are active

learn.concept: A credential attack noisy enough to lock accounts hits MANY accounts from ONE source — vs the single-user stale-cred case. Correlate 4771/4776 to the source: external + many accounts + no RoE = active attack, not a misconfigured device.
learn.pointer: MITRE ATT&CK T1110 · lockout as spray collateral

cases.trigger: Ten accounts locked out within a few minutes, all failing from one source.
cases.why: Not a stale-cred misconfig: the 4771/4776 failures span 10+ accounts from a single external IP flagged on a credential-attack feed, foreign, with no authorized-testing ticket — noisy enough to lock each account. That's an active credential attack, and the lockouts are collateral. Escalate to IR and block the source. The tell vs the stale-cred case: MANY accounts from ONE external source, not one user's own device.

cases.alertTitle: Lockouts across accounts from an internal host
cases.detectionRule: SIEM · Event 4740 across ≥15 accounts from one source

evidence.detail: A signed pentest RoE covers credential testing from PENTEST-01 this week — lockouts are noted as an accepted side-effect.
evidence.label: Approved pentest RoE CHG-4130

evidence.detail: 4771/4776 failures across 18 accounts from PENTEST-01 (internal, security-team segment) — a spray, which is exactly what the engagement does.
evidence.label: Spray from the internal test host

evidence.detail: 4740 across many accounts; correlation points at the internal test host, not an external attacker.
evidence.label: Source correlates to PENTEST-01

evidence.detail: Internal source; nothing external in play.
evidence.label: Internal source

evidence.detail: The security calendar shows an authorized engagement running this week — consistent with the RoE.
evidence.label: Engagement window on the calendar

learn.concept: A sanctioned pentest can trip lockouts too — real spray behaviour, but authorized. Check the RoE / deconfliction before escalating a mass-lockout event; source-internal + a signed engagement = Benign-TP, same detection as the malicious spray.
learn.pointer: Purple-team deconfliction · 'is this us or someone else?'

cases.trigger: A burst of lockouts across 18 accounts, all failing from one internal host.
cases.why: It looks exactly like the malicious case — a spray causing lockouts across 18 accounts — and it IS spray behaviour, so the detection is correct. But the source is the security team's internal test host, and a signed pentest RoE covers it (lockouts noted as an accepted side-effect). Correct detection of authorized activity = Benign-TP: confirm the RoE, note it, close benign. Escalating would burn IR on a sanctioned test.

cases.alertTitle: Insider risk — departing-employee data theft
cases.detectionRule: Purview IRM · 'Data theft by departing users' (High)

evidence.detail: HR: jwalsh resigned; last working day is Friday. IRM's departing-user policy is scoring exfiltration indicators against that end date.
evidence.label: Departing — last day Friday

evidence.detail: A sequence: bulk SharePoint downloads, then copies to a personal cloud account and a USB, this week — well above jwalsh's 90-day baseline.
evidence.label: Download-then-exfiltrate to a PERSONAL account

evidence.detail: No approved bulk-export, data-migration, or offboarding-handover ticket covers this activity.
evidence.label: No authorized export

evidence.detail: The files match the customer-list / pricing DLP policy — sensitive, and far above a Sales rep's normal export volume.
evidence.label: Sensitive customer data, above norm

evidence.detail: Several accessed folders sit outside jwalsh's team's normal scope.
evidence.label: Some access is out of scope

evidence.detail: No external indicators — this is a trusted insider, not an outside attacker. That's exactly why it's hard: the account is legitimate.
evidence.label: Nothing external to enrich

learn.concept: Insider threat is the archetype where the action alone tells you nothing — the same download is malicious or benign depending on intent, authorization and role. Read CONTEXT: employment status (departing?), an authorized-export ticket, and whether the data is in scope. And the disposition inverts the usual instinct: ESCALATE to a multi-stakeholder insider-risk / HR / legal program — do NOT isolate or confront. A Tier-1 hands it up.
learn.pointer: Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management · CISA Insider Threat Mitigation Guide

cases.trigger: IRM flagged jwalsh (resignation on file, last day Friday): a spike of SharePoint bulk-downloads and copies to a personal cloud account this week.
cases.why: The subtlest archetype: the SAME bulk-download is theft or business-as-usual depending on AUTHORIZATION and ROLE. Here every discriminator points to theft — jwalsh resigned (last day Friday), there's a download-then-exfiltrate sequence to a personal cloud + USB well above baseline, on sensitive customer data, with no authorized-export ticket. Escalate to the insider-risk / HR / legal program — and do NOT unilaterally isolate or confront: that's an HR/legal matter, and tipping them off or acting alone destroys the case. Hand it up; preserve the evidence.

cases.alertTitle: Insider risk — bulk dataset access, user rmehta
cases.detectionRule: Purview IRM · anomalous activity above baseline (Medium)

evidence.detail: rmehta is a data scientist — large dataset access is squarely in scope. A data-heavy role has a high normal, so this isn't actually anomalous for them.
evidence.label: Large dataset access IS the job

evidence.detail: rmehta's 90-day baseline already includes regular large pulls; this week is within their normal range, prior history clean, no employment-status change.
evidence.label: Within their 90-day baseline

evidence.detail: Everything stays in the corporate analytics environment — no USB, no personal cloud, no external sharing.
evidence.label: Stays in the corporate environment

evidence.detail: A long-tenured active employee; no resignation or end-date signal.
evidence.label: Long-tenured, not departing

evidence.detail: Routine analytics; no special ticket, but none is needed for in-role access.
evidence.label: In-role work, no special ticket needed

evidence.detail: DLP matched on volume — which is what tripped the anomaly — but volume alone isn't the story for this role.
evidence.label: Matched on volume

learn.concept: UEBA insider anomalies over-fire on data-heavy roles — a data scientist's 'anomalous' bulk access is their baseline. Read role/scope + the user's own 90-day norm, not the raw volume. Same action, opposite verdict from the departing-employee case.
learn.pointer: Purview IRM · behavioral baselines · tune per-role thresholds

cases.trigger: IRM flagged rmehta for a spike in large dataset downloads this week.
cases.why: The mirror of the departing-employee case: the SAME bulk access, opposite verdict. rmehta is a data scientist — large dataset access is their JOB, in scope, and within their 90-day baseline; it stays in the corporate environment; they're not departing. The UEBA 'anomaly' misfired because a data-heavy role has a high normal. Close FP and tune the baseline for the role. The action told you nothing — role and context did.

cases.alertTitle: Insider risk — large export to cloud, user tokafor
cases.detectionRule: Purview IRM · 'Data leaks' (High-severity DLP)

evidence.detail: An approved data-migration change authorizes moving this records set to the new CORPORATE cloud tenant this week; tokafor is the assigned migration engineer.
evidence.label: Approved migration CHG-5330

evidence.detail: The export goes to the corporate tenant (the migration target), not a personal account — a real bulk export, but the sanctioned one.
evidence.label: To the corporate tenant, not personal

evidence.detail: tokafor is on the migrations team; this records set is in scope for the project.
evidence.label: Migrations engineer, in scope

evidence.detail: Active employee; no resignation or end-date signal.
evidence.label: Active, not departing

evidence.detail: DLP matched on volume/class correctly: it genuinely is a large sensitive export (the detection is right).
evidence.label: Correctly matched — it IS a big export

evidence.detail: No prior insider-risk history; nothing correlating with employment status.
evidence.label: No prior risk history

learn.concept: A sanctioned bulk export / migration is a Benign-TP: the detection correctly fires on a real large transfer, but a change ticket authorizes it and the destination is corporate, not personal. Distinguish the three: role-baseline (FP — the anomaly never happened) vs authorized migration (Benign-TP — it happened, and a ticket sanctioned it) vs departing-employee theft (TP — unauthorized, personal destination, leaving).
learn.pointer: Purview IRM · authorized-export / migration exclusion

cases.trigger: IRM flagged tokafor for a large one-off export of a records set to cloud storage.
cases.why: Unlike the role-baseline FP, this IS a real, above-baseline bulk export — the detection is correct — but it's the sanctioned migration: an approved change ticket, tokafor is the assigned engineer, and the destination is the CORPORATE tenant, not a personal account. Correct detection of authorized activity = Benign-TP: confirm the ticket, note it, close benign. The discriminators vs the departing-employee theft: authorization + corporate destination + in-role, and the user isn't leaving.

evidence.detail: An authorized engagement / RoE (RoE-PLR-14) covers this operator, target and window. The activity is real attack behaviour — but sanctioned.

learn.concept: Same board, two seats: a red-team run seen from the blue chair. The ONLY thing separating a Benign-TP from a TP is authorization — check for the engagement / RoE / deconfliction record before you act, not who the tradecraft looks like. That's exactly why those records exist.
